source: SLSA v0.1 Threat Model (Threats and Mitigations, detailed)

rules.name: Submit Unauthorized Change Without Review
rules.description: An adversary pushes a change directly to the source repository, bypassing peer review entirely (e.g. pushing straight to main without a pull request).

rules.name: Self-Review via Sock Puppet Account
rules.description: An adversary proposes a change from one account and approves it using a second, colluding account they also control, satisfying a two-person review requirement in appearance only.

rules.name: Exploit Robot Account to Bypass Review
rules.description: An adversary compromises an automated (robot) account that is permitted to submit changes without human review, then uses it to introduce malicious code.

rules.name: Abuse Review Exceptions
rules.description: An adversary exploits a carve-out in the review policy (e.g. an exemption for documentation-only changes) to smuggle in an executable or malicious file that technically qualifies for the exception.

rules.name: Modify Code After Review Without Invalidating Approval
rules.description: An adversary gets a benign change approved, then silently modifies it before merging, if the platform does not invalidate stale approvals on new pushes.

rules.name: Submit an Unreviewable Change
rules.description: An adversary crafts a change that is technically presented for review but structured (e.g. a hash-only diff) so the reviewer cannot meaningfully evaluate its actual content.

rules.name: Copy a Reviewed Change to a Different Context
rules.description: An adversary gets a change reviewed in a low-trust context (e.g. a personal fork) and then transfers or merges it into a higher-trust context without requiring fresh review there.

rules.name: Compromise a Trusted Account
rules.description: An adversary gains access to a legitimate contributor's account (e.g. via a weak or reused password) and uses it to submit and approve their own malicious changes.

rules.name: Hide a Bad Change Behind a Good One
rules.description: An adversary submits a sequence of commits where an early commit introduces malicious behavior and a later commit appears to undo it, so a reviewer approving the final state unknowingly also approves the hidden malicious intermediate revision.

rules.name: Project Owner Bypasses Repository Controls
rules.description: A trusted person with administrative privileges disables branch protection or review requirements, pushes unreviewed code, and optionally re-enables the controls afterward to hide the bypass.

rules.name: Platform Administrator Abuses Privileges
rules.description: An employee or insider at the hosting platform (e.g. a git hosting provider) uses internal tooling to push unauthorized or malicious changes to a repository, potentially targeting specific consumers while hiding the change from others.

rules.name: Build from an Unofficial Source Fork
rules.description: A build is performed using the expected CI/CD pipeline, but pointed at an unofficial fork of the repository that may contain unauthorized changes not present in the canonical source.

rules.name: Build from an Unofficial Branch or Tag
rules.description: A build uses the correct repository and pipeline, but checks out an unprotected experimental branch instead of the officially released branch, pulling in code not intended for release.

rules.name: Build Using Unofficial Build Steps
rules.description: A build runs on the legitimate CI/CD platform but substitutes custom, unofficial build instructions in place of the build steps defined in the source repository.

rules.name: Build from an Unofficial Entry Point
rules.description: A build uses the correct pipeline, source, and branch, but triggers an unintended workflow or entry point (e.g. a debug workflow) rather than the official release workflow.

rules.name: Build from Source Modified After Checkout
rules.description: An adversary fetches the source, makes a local, unrecorded modification, and requests a build from that locally-modified copy rather than directly from the official repository.

rules.name: Inject Malicious Behavior via Build Parameters
rules.description: An adversary supplies a build parameter (e.g. a custom compiler flag) to an otherwise legitimate build pipeline that injects malicious behavior into the resulting output.

rules.name: Persist Compromise Across Builds (Non-Ephemeral Environment)
rules.description: An adversary tampers with a build environment (e.g. replacing a system tool) during one build, and that tampering silently persists to affect subsequent, otherwise-legitimate builds on the same machine.

rules.name: Compromise a Parallel Build (Lack of Build Isolation)
rules.description: An adversary runs a malicious build concurrently with a legitimate build on shared infrastructure, tampering with the legitimate build's inputs or outputs while it runs.

rules.name: Steal Build Signing Secrets
rules.description: An adversary who controls a build worker exfiltrates or misuses the cryptographic key used to sign build provenance, allowing them to forge authentic-looking attestations for malicious builds.

rules.name: Falsify Provenance Values from a Compromised Worker
rules.description: An adversary who controls a build worker (rather than the trusted control plane) fabricates false information in the build provenance, e.g. claiming the build came from a different, legitimate-looking source repository.

rules.name: Poison the Build Cache
rules.description: An adversary inserts a malicious artifact into a shared build cache under a falsified cache key, causing a later, legitimate build to unknowingly reuse the poisoned artifact.

rules.name: Build Using an Untrusted CI/CD Platform
rules.description: A package is built using an unofficial or lower-trust CI/CD service instead of the expected, more rigorously secured build platform, and the weaker platform is then exploited to inject bad behavior.

rules.name: Upload a Package Without Provenance
rules.description: An adversary uploads a malicious package version to a registry without any accompanying build provenance, hoping consumers do not require or check for it.

rules.name: Tamper with a Built Artifact After the Fact
rules.description: An adversary takes a legitimately built package, modifies its contents, and re-uploads the modified artifact while reusing the original, now-mismatched provenance record.

rules.name: Forge or Tamper with Provenance Metadata
rules.description: An adversary performs a build that would not pass verification policy as-is, then alters the accompanying provenance document to make the build appear compliant.

rules.name: Typosquatting (Explicitly Out of Scope for SLSA)
rules.description: An adversary publishes a malicious package under a name closely resembling a popular, legitimate package to trick users into installing it. SLSA's own specification notes this threat is largely outside its scope, though source-availability requirements can mildly aid detection.

rules.name: Delete Source Revision to Prevent Inspection
rules.description: An adversary builds from a malicious source revision, then deletes or force-overwrites that revision's history, preventing anyone from later inspecting what was actually built.

rules.name: Dependency Becomes Unavailable
rules.description: A dependency required by the build process is removed, taken offline, or otherwise made unavailable, disrupting the ability to reproduce or continue building the software (an availability, not integrity, threat).

rules.name: Tamper with Verification Policy Itself
rules.description: An adversary modifies the acceptance policy used to verify provenance (e.g. adding a malicious source repository to the allow-list), enabling subsequent malicious builds to pass verification.

rules.name: Forge Change Metadata
rules.description: An adversary falsifies the authorship, timestamp, or history of a source change to obscure attribution or make a malicious change appear older and more trustworthy than it is.

rules.name: Exploit Cryptographic Hash Collisions
rules.description: An adversary exploits a weakness in the hash function used for code review or provenance verification to submit a malicious artifact that collides with the hash of a previously-reviewed, benign one.
